claim: The plaintiffs, as administrators of the estate of the deceased, brought the present action for damages against the defendants.
requested_remedy: The plaintiffs, as administrators of the estate of the deceased, brought the present action for damages against the defendants.
parties: Plaintiff: CHEUNG KOON HO administratrix and CHEUNG KOON YUNG
Defendant: ICOS VIBRO LTD., YUN CHAK CONSTRUCTION AND ENGINEERING CO., WU YAU CO.

facts.F1: The deceased Lee Wai Wan commenced a new job as a caisson worker on a construction site at Taikoo Shing on 6th October 1982.
facts.F2: He was a married man, aged 24 and the father of two young daughters.
facts.F3: The family lived in a wooden hut at Sai Wan Hoi together with the deceased’s parents.
facts.F4: The deceased had not previously been employed as a caisson worker.
facts.F5: On the fourth day of work, the deceased was being brought up the well when he fell from the bucket to the bottom of the well and died.
facts.F6: The bucket was used for two purposes, to bring up spoil excavated by the male worker and to convey the male worker up and down the well during the course of his work.
facts.F7: The deceased and Madam Ng had been working together on one particular caisson for 4 days.
facts.F8: The deceased was the male member of one such team and Madam Ng Yau was the female member of that team.
facts.F9: The deceased was employed by the 3rd defendant, WU YAU CO.
facts.F10: The contract for the construction of the caissons had been let to the 1st defendant which subcontracted the work to the 2nd defendant which in turn further subcontracted the work to the 3rd defendant.
facts.F11: The defendants failed to provide a means of egress and ingress to the caisson which was safe and free from danger.
facts.F12: The defendants knew that workmen customarily followed the unlawful practice of standing on the rim of the bucket.
facts.F13: The deceased's family would have reduced expenses due to his death.

facts.F1: The plaintiff, Mr Chan, purchased a property called House Type 4A, No.10 of Gmelina Path, Palm Springs, Phase 1C in the New Territories (the Property) for $12.18 million under a provisional agreement dated 20 September 1997.
facts.F2: At the time of purchase, the property market in Hong Kong was very active, and many speculators, including Mr Chan, would give blank cheques and blank signed provisional agreements to estate agents to buy a property that could be quickly resold for a profit.
facts.F3: The plaintiff instructed the estate agent, Mr Wong, to find a property worth not more than $13 million and with a size of not less than 2000 sq. ft.
facts.F4: The defendant signed the provisional agreement on 20 September 1997 after being persuaded by Mr Wong.
facts.F5: The plaintiff did not see the Property before purchasing it, which was common practice among speculators in Hong Kong at the time.
facts.F6: The next day, the plaintiff, his wife, and another lady visited the Property with Mr Wong and saw the garden, various parts of the house, and a fibre glass structure on the roof that was not authorized by the manager of the building.
facts.F7: The plaintiff knew that the structure was unauthorised and might be removed by the manager, but he still wanted to retain it.
facts.F8: A supplemental agreement was signed on 8 October 1997 to retain the fibre glass structure on the roof.
facts.F9: The plaintiff tried to resell the house for a quick profit but failed due to a decline in the market price.
facts.F10: A notice was served by the manager to remove the fibre glass structure, and the plaintiff relied on clause 23(a) of the formal sale and purchase agreement to rescind the agreement and claim back his deposit.
facts.F11: There was an agreement contained in the document at p.206 that required the vendor to retain the fibre glass structure.
facts.F12: There was a document at p.207 that handed over the keys to the premises to the plaintiff and required him to assume all responsibilities, including paying all outgoings.

facts.F1: The plaintiffs agreed to lend the 1st defendant or alternatively the 1st and 2nd defendants the sum of $6,350,000.00 plus interest, with the security for this loan being the Panama vessel m.v. Eastland Trader, later to be named the m.v. San Antonio, then being converted into a bulk carrier.
facts.F2: The agreement was set out in a letter dated 10th September 1966 (Document 8 in the agreed bundle of documents).
facts.F3: On 14th September 1966, the defendants wrote a letter (Document 11 in the agreed bundle of documents) jointly guaranteed by the 1st and 2nd defendants and personally guaranteed by the 3rd defendant.
facts.F4: On 30th December 1966, the plaintiffs exercised their option to purchase the m.v. Eastland Trader, later to be named the m.v. San Antonio, but did not purchase the vessel under a Memorandum of Agreement.
facts.F5: The m.v. San Antonio was surveyed by Mr. J.G. Pasteuning, the representative of the Bureau Veritas in Hong Kong, who issued a provisional certificate dated 28th December 1966.
facts.F6: The Bureau Veritas issued their Certificate of Classification on 25th May 1967, which included two requirements to be fulfilled at the latest at the next annual survey of the ship.
facts.F7: The plaintiffs had the required work done on the vessel by the Hakodate Dock Company in Japan from 18th January to 25th January 1968, at the cost of $9,843,050 Japanese yen, equivalent to HK$166,972:01.
facts.F8: The 1st defendant acknowledged the receipt of the letter exercising the option to purchase and added an endorsement that the defendants would complete any outstanding recommendations by the Bureau Veritas when the vessel returned to Hong Kong.
facts.F9: The conversion of the vessel to the entire satisfaction of the Bureau Veritas of Shipping with Special Survey passed in Hong Kong meant satisfaction at the time of the survey, not in perpetuity.
facts.F10: The Bureau Veritas was entirely satisfied with the conversion of the vessel on 28th December 1966 as evidenced by the provisional certificate issued by Mr. J.G. Pasteuning.
facts.F11: The vessel was not brought back to Hong Kong for the work to be performed.
